items.title: AI leadership readiness profiles and competence gaps among school leaders during digital transformation: a comparative study of China and Kazakhstan
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a school-level governance issue during digital transformation, yet how school leaders translate instructional judgments into implementation readiness remains insufficiently understood. This cross-national study examined AI leadership readiness in China and Kazakhstan, focusing on scenario understanding, instructional value, risk concern, digital leadership self-efficacy, organizational support, leadership support for adoption, implementation readiness, and competence gaps. Methods We analyzed a cross-national quantitative survey of 763 school leaders (China n = 389; Kazakhstan n = 374) using reliability analysis, measurement invariance testing, latent profile analysis, standardized recursive path modeling, and importance–competence gap analysis. Results Internal consistency was adequate for most constructs; AI-related risk concern was lower (α = 0.581, ω = 0.582). Scalar invariance met conventional fit-change criteria, and observed composite scores were higher among Chinese respondents for scenario understanding, instructional value, leadership support, digital leadership self-efficacy, and implementation readiness, whereas risk concern was higher among Kazakhstani respondents. The retained four-profile solution comprised high understanding–high readiness, value-positive–near-average readiness, risk-sensitive cautious, and low understanding–low readiness. Scenario understanding was positively associated with instructional value (β = 0.585); instructional value was positively associated with leadership support (β = 0.339); and digital leadership self-efficacy was positively associated with implementation readiness (β = 0.328). The largest importance–competence gaps concerned ethics and risk governance ( G = 1.75), teacher development ( G = 1.58), and content quality audit ( G = 1.56). Discussion Positive instructional appraisals frequently coexisted with moderate school-level preparation. Implementation readiness was most closely associated with digital leadership self-efficacy, organizational support, and leadership support for adoption. Ethics and risk governance, teacher development, and content quality audit emerged as the leading priorities for professional learning.

items.title: AI-BASED ACTIVITIES FOR DEVELOPING SPEAKING SKILLS
items.abstract: Developing speaking skills is one of the most challenging aspects of learning English as a foreign language (EFL). Many learners lack opportunities to communicate in English outside the classroom and face challenges such as anxiety, a lack of confidence, limited vocabulary, and difficulty formulating spontaneous speech. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new opportunities for independent speaking practice through AI-based speaking partners. This article focuses on the potential of AI partners to enhance English speaking skills, specifically highlighting platforms such as IELTS.gg (now GoPrep) and CEFRbek. The discussion centers on how AI partners can provide convenient, flexible, low-anxiety, and personalized speaking practice.

items.title: AI-Based Career Recommendation System for Students
items.abstract: This paper studies how an AI-Based Career Recommendation System can be designed, built and deployed for students who struggle to pick a suitable academic or professional path. Because work is changing quickly with new technology, conventional counselling often cannot give guidance that is individualised, data-based and current. The proposed system uses machine learning algorithms, data mining techniques and natural language processing (NLP) models to assess a student's marks, behaviour, interests, personality and skills. Data from psychometric tests, academic records, interest inventories and career knowledge bases is combined so the system can suggest options that fit each learner's strengths and the openings in the job market. Since it detects patterns and estimates future career fit, it is expected to advise more accurately than manual counselling. The paper also stresses adaptive models that keep learning from user interactions, so suggestions improve with use. The system further seeks to lessen student uncertainty, support informed choices, and give institutions an efficient, scalable counselling service. Ultimately, the work shows that artificial intelligence can reshape career guidance, making it more individual, efficient and in step with industry trends.

items.title: AI-Driven Federated Learning for Securing the Internet of Medical Things: A Critical Review of Architectures, Threats, and Blockchain-Enabled Trust
items.abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has become central to modern healthcare by enabling continuous patient monitoring and real-time clinical decision-making, yet the rapid proliferation of connected medical devices has simultaneously expanded the attack surface and introduced serious risks to patient safety. While artificial intelligence offers strong capabilities for detecting and mitigating cyber threats, conventional centralized AI approaches often require the collection and processing of sensitive patient data, thereby recreating the very privacy risks they aim to solve. Federated learning addresses this limitation by allowing multiple devices or institutions to collaboratively train a shared model without exchanging raw data; however, it remains vulnerable to malicious or poisoned model updates from untrusted participants and still faces unresolved challenges of trust and accountability. Blockchain has been proposed as a complementary mechanism to establish decentralized trust and enhance the auditability of federated environments, although evidence of its scalability and practical feasibility in real-world healthcare settings remains limited. This paper critically examines the current landscape of security solutions at the intersection of AI, federated learning, blockchain, and IoMT. Drawing on a curated body of recent research, it maps the IoMT threat landscape across network, model, and privacy dimensions; compares AI-driven, federated, and blockchain-enabled approaches; and synthesizes findings across key technical criteria including threat coverage, detection capability, privacy protection, trust management, communication efficiency, scalability, and practical deployment feasibility. The analysis reveals three persistent gaps: inconsistent reporting practices, fragmented and heterogeneous datasets, and an unresolved tension between claimed blockchain efficiency and the limited empirical support for its scalability in real clinical environments. Notably, no existing study jointly evaluates AI, FL, and blockchain under standardized conditions that reflect a realistic hospital IoMT deployment. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a research agenda focused on real-world scalability validation, regulatory-aligned privacy standardization, 6G-integrated architectures, explainability-by-default, and quantum-resilient federated learning, with the goal of advancing IoMT security solutions that are technically robust, trustworthy, scalable, and patient-centric. Keywords : Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), federated learning, artificial intelligence, blockchain, intrusion detection, privacy-preserving machine learning.

items.title: AI-Driven Voice Intelligence for Pandemic and Disaster Preparedness: A Scoping Review and Development of a National Emergency Communication Framework
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered voice technologies have emerged as valuable tools in enhancing crisis communication during pandemics and disasters, yet their use in the United States (U.S.) remains fragmented. This scoping review identified and mapped evidence on AI-enabled voice intelligence for pandemic and disaster response in the U.S. and developed an evidence-informed National Voice Intelligence Emergency Preparedness Framework (NVIEPF). The review was carried out based on the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidance. The literature was searched from key bibliographic databases and grey literature sources between January 2015 and May 2026. Fifteen eligible records were synthesized using evidence mapping and thematic analysis. Current applications were primarily limited to speech recognition, automatic transcription, conversational agents, multilingual communication, and decision support in public safety communication systems. The biggest challenges were the lack of a unified communication system, the lack of consistency in implementation, limited interoperability, governance issues, cybersecurity issues, and the lack of proper evaluation in operational contexts. This research contributed to the conceptualization of the NVIEPF, which has five interconnected components that involve AI-based early warning, crisis communication, surveillance, resource coordination, and community feedback, all with human oversight. The evidence was limited by its reliance on programme reports, observational studies, and operational documentation, with limited evaluation in real-world emergency settings. Although evidence of widespread adoption of AI-driven voice technologies is limited, the framework provides a means for future research, policy development, and a phased approach to integrating AI-powered voice intelligence into the national preparedness system in the U.S.

items.title: AI-Generated versus Official Subtitles in Documentary Translation: A Literature Review Based on Season 2 of the Potala Palace
items.abstract: Comparisons between machine-generated renderings and official subtitles are accumulating, yet it remains unclear where the two diverge in documentary subtitling, a genre in which the image carries part of the meaning. This review examines 25 items bearing on that question: 17 Chinese journal articles, six monographs, one dissertation, and one web source, 12 of them published after 2020, retrieved from CNKI and through reference-list tracing. Four lines of research are distinguished: comparisons of machine and human translation, the constraints of subtitling, documentary subtitle research, and translation quality assessment. Three findings emerge. First, the studies reviewed broadly agree that machine output is no longer inferior to human translation in semantic fidelity, and that its weaknesses concentrate in fluency, terminological consistency, and contextual cohesion. Second, most of these studies argue from illustrative examples rather than item-level counts and explicit criteria, so their conclusions are hard to verify. Third, research on subtitles has described the constraints of the medium in detail, and international work has turned them into computable parameters such as line limits and characters per second. A gap follows from the three. Existing comparisons treat the official translation as the sole standard, without separating genuine mistranslation from legitimate variation. The coordination of subtitles with the image, and the consistency of proper-name renderings across a whole film, has rarely been examined within the scope of this search. The review therefore proposes a three-way alignment that takes the source text and the image as joint reference, and a three-level scheme of judgement — word-and-sentence, contextual, and whole-film — counted level by level. Both are illustrated with three examples from Season 2 of the documentary The Potala Palace, in order to delimit what current large language models can and cannot achieve here.

items.title: ALADIN PRIM v01: Conserved-to-Primitive Conversion with a Derived and Verified Pressure Error Bound for a Native-Cylindrical GPU MHD Driver (Kernel 01, Campaign PRIM-01)
items.abstract: PRIM v01 is kernel 01 of the ALADIN native-cylindrical GPU MHD Driver for Z-pinch and J×B research. It converts the conserved state (ρ, m, E) and the constrained-transport face magnetic field into primitive variables (ρ, v, p). It is one CUDA/C++ source that runs on the GPU through NVRTC and on the CPU through g++/OpenMP, in FP64 and FP32. What PRIM provides: A pressure error bound in every cell. PRIM returns b with |p − p_exact| ≤ b·p. The bound is derived by rounding-error analysis, with its assumptions stated, and verified numerically against an 80-bit oracle in both the normal and the subnormal range. A cell is flagged UNRESOLVED when p keeps fewer than 3 significant digits, as happens at low plasma β. Refusal instead of floors. Three kinds of cell are refused, with NaN outputs and a flag: non-positive density or any non-finite input; total energy below kinetic plus magnetic energy; finite inputs whose intermediates overflow. The adiabatic index must satisfy 1 < γ ≤ 2. An explicit flag policy for the Driver, consistent with HLLD v05.1. A consistent cell-centred field. It is the constrained-transport face average, the same one HLLD v05.1 and UCT-EMF v02 use. Bit-identical GPU and CPU results, including the subnormal range. An inverse, conserved(), which converts primitive variables back to the conserved state. Results (campaign PRIM-01, run 4): GPU leg (NVIDIA L4) 17 / 17 VERIFIED; CPU leg 11 / 11 VERIFIED. compute-sanitizer: 0 errors and 0 hazards. The pressure bound is never exceeded. The worst case uses 0.32 of the bound over 758 733 normal-range cells (ρ from 1e-8 to 1e8, β from 1e-12 to 1e6) and 0.29 over 375 k underflow-range cells. Every velocity is the correctly rounded m/ρ. Refusal is exact and local, and overflow is refused. GPU = CPU bit for bit, in the normal and the subnormal range. The README normalised Z-pinch is recovered to 1.1e-16, and HLLD fed with PRIM’s output keeps exact balance. In FP32, p keeps 3 digits only down to β ≈ 1e-4; in FP64, down to β ≈ 1e-12. Development record: publication review of run 1 led to overflow refusal, γ validation, underflow terms in the bound and the written derivation (run 2). Run 2 then failed in FP32 on the GPU. Diagnosis traced the failure to CuPy’s RawModule, which appends -ftz=true after user options and so flushes FP32 subnormals whatever the user passes. Run 4 compiles through NVRTC directly and checks the PTX. All runs and probes are preserved. The bundle contains the kernel, the independent oracle, the campaign with predeclared thresholds, both legs’ results, the sanitizer logs, the Driver adapter, the README benchmark, the full history, and the verification report. items.title: An agentic-AI calibrate–diagnose–suggest workflow for parameter identification in soil constitutive models
items.abstract: Calibration of advanced soil constitutive models remains challenging because multiple parameters jointly control stress–strain responses. In practice, these parameters are often determined by manual trial and error from a few laboratory tests, leaving two questions unanswered: whether the fitted parameters are identifiable and which additional test would best reduce the remaining ambiguity. A parameter set may therefore reproduce the available data yet remain non-unique, leading to divergent predictions under untested conditions. In this work, we develop a human-supervised agentic-AI calibrate–diagnose–suggest workflow for parameter identification in soil constitutive models. The workflow combines gradient-based parameter estimation, Fisher-information-based diagnosis of weak parameter directions, and a large language model (LLM) agent that translates the weakest Fisher direction into a targeted follow-up laboratory test. This translation is guided by an LLM-organized parameter–response map, which is checked against established expert guidance. We demonstrate the workflow using NorSand in eight simulator-generated triaxial scenarios spanning drainage conditions, density states, and confining pressures. A single agent-suggested follow-up test substantially reduces the broad multi-parameter ambiguity left by single-test calibration: excluding one weakly observable parameter, the median relative error is 0.17%, and Fisher information analysis indicates improved local identifiability in all eight scenarios. The workflow also exposes the parameter that fit-only calibration would leave weakly constrained. We further find that a complementary test selected retrospectively from published data reduces local ambiguity in the targeted parameter combination. These findings show that agentic AI can support auditable calibration by turning numerical identifiability diagnosis into actionable decisions.

items.title: An artificial intelligence-driven virtual patient for communication skills training in medical education: an exploratory pilot study of usability and perceived educational value
items.abstract: Background Effective communication is a core competency in medical education, but traditional training is resource-intensive and hard to scale. Virtual patients based on large language models (LLMs) may help, yet evidence on their usability and perceived value outside English-language settings is limited. Methods In this cross-sectional pilot study, 102 medical students at the University of Málaga completed two Spanish-language history-taking encounters with a GPT-4-based virtual patient and received automated feedback. They completed an anonymous, self-developed questionnaire (0–10 ratings and open-ended questions). Analyses were descriptive, plus an exploratory logistic regression of gender on perceived training need. Results Participants were mostly women (73.5%) and fourth-year students (85.3%). 86.3% (88/102) rated the tool easy or very easy to use and 60.8% (62/102) reported no need for prior training. Most feedback statements had mean ratings of 7.4 or more (0–10), highest for usefulness in exploring the reason for consultation and the patient's history (8.3); agreement that AI feedback does not replace tutors was moderate (6.14). Women were less likely than men to report needing prior training (OR: 0.29, 95% CI: 0.11–0.73; exploratory hypothesis-generating). Free-text comments ( n = 33) valued realism, interaction and feedback depth, and noted limited case variety and no nonverbal communication. Conclusions Students found the LLM-based virtual patient easy to use and its feedback useful. Given the lack of a comparison group, non-validated self-report measures, a single site and co-first authors affiliation with the developer, the findings indicate acceptability and perceived value only, not effectiveness. Controlled studies with validated, observer-rated outcomes are needed.
